subtopic: Handling a leaked photo or online harassment
subtype: Approach: staying calm and not replying in anger [Thinking]
passage: The photo appeared in the class group at twenty to ten: a private one of Pranav, meant for a single friend. His face went hot, then cold. His thumbs were already typing, Who did this??? and worse. He looked at the words, then deleted them. If he fired back, they would screenshot that too, and it would become a fight instead of a wrong done to him. He put the phone face down and breathed until his hands stopped shaking. Then he called his cousin Kunal, who told him, “Don't answer anyone. Go to your mother now.” Pranav walked into the living room. His mother listened, put an arm round him, said, “This is not your fault,” and picked up the phone to call the school's safety lead that night.

qa.q: What did Pranav do with the angry message he typed?
What was Pranav feeling when the photo appeared?
qa.a: Panic and rage: his face went hot, then cold, and his thumbs began typing angry words.

qa.q: What could Pranav do next, and why?
qa.a: Save screenshots with dates and share them with the school, since adults can act on real proof.

qa.q: How does the night look to Pranav's mother?
qa.a: Pranav's mother is shocked and worried but glad he came to her, and phoning the school safety lead the same night gives her something useful to do.

grounding: A teen who sees a private photo shared in a class group decides an angry reply would fuel it and goes to an adult first.

subtopic: Handling a leaked photo or online harassment
subtype: Approach: staying calm and not replying in anger [Thinking]
passage:
“Tanu Di, look.” Yusuf pushed his phone across the bed. His hands were shaking.
Tanuja read the class group. A photo of him asleep at last week's sleepover, mouth open, in his old cartoon pyjamas. Under it, a caption about babies and forty-one laughing reactions.
“Who posted it?”
“Some account I don't know. But it was taken at Faisal's house.” His voice rose. “I'm going to write something so bad that they'll—”
“What would you write?”
He stopped. Typed. Deleted. “If I reply angry, they get a second show. They'll screenshot my reply and laugh at that too.”
“So what's the first step?”
“Not fighting. Getting help.” He breathed out slowly. “Screenshots first. Then Ammi and Abbu, tonight.”
“Ammi's in the kitchen right now. Come. I'll stand with you.”
Ammi read the screenshots twice, then put an arm round him. “You were right not to answer. Tonight we report the account, and tomorrow I call your class teacher first thing.”

qa.q: How many laughing reactions were under the photo?
What was Yusuf feeling when he started to type a reply?
qa.a: Yusuf felt humiliated and furious, hands shaking and voice rising, wanting to hit back with words.

qa.q: What else could Yusuf do instead of replying, and why is it better?
qa.a: Save screenshots and let adults report the account and speak to the school, because a reply only gives the group a second show.

qa.q: How might Ammi see Yusuf coming to her that night?
qa.a: Ammi is likely hurt for him but relieved he came straight to her, and ready to back him with the report and the school.

grounding: Shows a teen who feels panic and rage over a mocking photo in the class group deciding that an angry reply would feed it and that getting help comes first.

subtopic: Handling a leaked photo or online harassment
subtype: Approach: staying calm and not replying in anger [Thinking]
passage:
Last winter someone posted a photo of me in our class group: me crying in the corridor the day my dog died, with a caption added. I'm Arnab, and I still remember the heat in my face, the shaking, the feeling that I would explode.
I opened the reply box and wrote three lines to Tanvir, who I was sure had done it. Every word was meant to hurt.
Then I thought: the second I post this, everyone stops looking at the photo and starts watching the fight. They'd screenshot my reply. It would become the bigger story. And I didn't even know it was Tanvir.
So I deleted it. I took a screenshot of the post instead and walked to the staffroom before lunch was over. Mrs D'Souza read it, sat me down, and called my mother from her desk. The post was gone by evening.

qa.q: Who did Arnab show the screenshot to?
What did Arnab feel on first seeing the photo?
qa.a: Arnab felt humiliated and enraged, face hot and shaking, as if about to explode.

qa.q: What made deleting the reply the wiser choice?
qa.a: An angry reply would have become the bigger story and might have hit the wrong person; reporting it brought real help the same day.

qa.q: How might Tanvir have been affected if the reply had been posted?
qa.a: Tanvir could have been accused in front of everyone without proof, hurting a classmate who may have done nothing and spreading the fight.

grounding: Shows a teen who feels rage over a hurtful photo in the class group reasoning that an angry reply would fuel it, and going for help instead.
